newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. to push grain complaint against EU at WTO.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to push grain complaint against EU at WTO.

text.p: U.S. officials said on Wednesday they would pursue their case at the World Trade Organisation against the European Union's grain tariff system in the next few weeks.

The officials were speaking after they withdrew a request to the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) for the immediate establishment of a panel to adjudicate whether the EU system violated the body's rules.
"It was just a technical matter. We will be renewing the request in the near future," one U.S. source told Reuters.
The DSB had been expected to approve creation of a panel at a meeting on Tuesday, but the U.S. trade mission in Geneva advised the WTO just before that it was holding off.

A panel, which would have six months to come up with a ruling, was originally requested by Washington in October 1995 after initial talks with Brussels on the new tariff system failed to resolve their differences.
The EU blocked the bid, saying consultations still had a chance of resolving the row.

The United States then agreed to further talks, and only renewed the request late last month, when it said it wanted the question treated urgently -- meaning a panel would have to return its findings in three months.
It argued that this was because the case involved perishable goods and also because the EU had not fulfilled commitments it had given which led to the renewed discussions.
Creation of a panel would have been automatic at Tuesday's DSB meeting since under WTO rules no country can block a request the second time round.
The EU tariff system is based on a reference price for tariffs on imported grains -- wheat, rye, barley, corn, sorghum and rice.
The United States argues this runs against agreements in the 1986-93 Uruguay Round of global trade negotiations which brought agricultural produce under world trade rules for the first time.
Washington argues that to conform to the rules EU tariffs should be calculated on a shipment-by-shipment basis, but Brussels says this would be impossible to control and open to fraud.
EU officials say they believe the system is in line with the rules, and last week expressed surprise at the U.S. decision to push on for a panel, saying discussions were still under way.
